headroom.short: The gap between what the fiscal rules allow you to borrow and what you are forecast to borrow. Your safety margin, and the score the game keeps.

fiscal-rules.short: Two rules the government set itself: pay for day-to-day spending out of tax by the target year, and get debt falling as a share of the economy.

obr.short: The Office for Budget Responsibility: the independent body that produces the official forecast and checks the Chancellor’s sums.

manifesto.short: The promises the party made at the election, such as not raising certain taxes. Breaking one is the fastest way to lose the public.

flagship.short: A headline policy that shows what the Budget is for. Each one here is a lever in the package with a price.

current-budget.short: Day-to-day spending set against tax revenue, leaving investment out. The stability rule says it must balance.

borrowing.short: The gap between what the government spends in a year and what it raises, covered by selling gilts.

debt.short: Everything the government owes, built up from past borrowing. The rules use a measure called net financial liabilities.

rpi.short: The Retail Prices Index, an older measure of inflation. Some government debt pays interest linked to it, so higher RPI costs the Treasury money.

gilts.short: UK government bonds: the IOUs the Treasury sells to borrow. When gilt yields rise, borrowing costs more.

welfare-cap.short: A ceiling on spending on most working-age benefits, set by the Treasury and monitored by the OBR.

fiscal-year.short: The government’s financial year, April to March. The year written 2029-30 runs from April 2029 to March 2030.

barnett.short: The formula that changes the Scottish, Welsh and Northern Irish budgets when comparable English spending changes.

hmrc-points.short: HMRC publishes what a tax change would raise at a few set sizes of change. Between those points the game draws a straight line, so a setting in between is an estimate.

spending-review.short: The exercise that fixed each department’s day-to-day budget for the next three years and its investment budget for four. This Budget starts from those settlements.

real-terms.short: After inflation. A budget that rises in cash but buys less because prices rose faster has fallen in real terms.

settlement.short: The budget a department was given at the Spending Review: how much it has to spend each year, in cash, for the years the review covers.

certified.short: A costing the OBR has checked and signed off as reasonable. The Treasury’s and HMRC’s published figures are certified; this game’s own arithmetic is not, and is badged as an assumption.

gdp.short: Gross domestic product: the size of the whole economy in a year. Debt and borrowing are judged as a share of it, because a bigger economy can carry more.

triple-lock.short: The state pension rises each April by the highest of prices, average earnings or a fixed minimum. The fixed minimum is what usually costs money.

pip.short: Personal Independence Payment: the main benefit for the extra costs of disability, paid whether or not someone works. Its caseload has grown fast and is hard to forecast.

nao.short: The National Audit Office: Parliament’s auditor, which reports on whether departments spend money well. Several ministers here quote its findings.

reserve.short: Money the Treasury holds back each year for things no department budgeted for. Spend it early and the next emergency has nothing to draw on.

uprating.short: Raising a benefit, a tax threshold or a duty each year, usually in line with prices or earnings. Freezing something instead is a quiet way of cutting it.

unprotected.short: A department whose budget has no promise attached. When the totals are squeezed, the unprotected departments take the cut, because health, defence and schools cannot.

escape-clause.short: The Charter lets a Chancellor suspend the fiscal rules in a significant shock. The OBR judges how severe the shock is; missing a rule by choice does not qualify.

protected.short: A department the OBR’s forecast holds to its settlement after the Spending Review years: health, defence and schools. When the totals are squeezed, the cut falls elsewhere.

earliest-start.short: The first tax year a measure could take effect on its own source’s timetable: legislation, systems, valuations or transitional protection. Nothing is counted before it, whatever start year the game uses.
